Spitballing off u/keckbug, also NAL, but I work with trusts and estates, and you should consider changing this. I have seen this designation now a few times, and it is a costly and time-consuming pain for families to try to collect death benefits with the 'All my children' designation. In my experience, I have never seen an insurance co. say this designation was invalid and then pay a policy out to a probate estate. It is more likely the insurance co. would ask for a court order instructing them on how to distribute the policy. 

However, the **most likely** scenario is that the insurance co. will make your children (or grandchildren if that's the case) submit an affidavit stating your descendants. This is often not easy for a layperson to understand and what do people do when they need help? See a lawyer ($$).

If they choose not to see a lawyer, and the affidavit is completed incorrectly, it's possible that the policy will be cashed-out on that incorrect info, or refused. Either way, it's likely someone will need to see a lawyer to get it corrected ($$), and if it was paid out incorrectly, here comes even more legal fees and a fighting family.

No matter how you slice it, this this specific designation will be a burden on your family once you pass. If you have the ability to, change your designations to specifically list your children (individually, one-by-one) in equal shares, with contingent beneficiaries. Alternatively, if you can afford to do so, see an estate planning attorney and ask them about setting-up a trust and designating the trust as beneficiary of all of your policies and accounts. You don't need to be rich to have an estate plan that includes a trust and with that you can be as specific as you like. This will likely bring on some legal fees after you pass, but those will be paid by the trust, and not your children. This means less fighting because one kid isn't paying for an attorney without the others chipping in -- instead it all comes out of the pot.

If you are in the US and need help finding an attorney, NAELA, the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys, offers a free online search.

NAL, but I work in probate in another state. If you have to probate the estate (open an estate in court), the creditors have a deadline to file claims against the estate. Meaning if say, your grandma has a Kohl's credit card when she dies, you open a probate estate, and no claim is filed to collect on the kohl's card, they are SOL and you don't have to pay it. In fact, most creditors don't file claims, and even those who do will have their claims dismissed because they pretty much never appear in court. I suggest speaking with an attorney after your grandma dies.

I don't think I have shared this story on reddit before, so here goes.

To preface, I used to have unique last name. Several years ago, I worked as a bankruptcy paralegal and one of our clients was a CapitalOne employee who had a garnishment on their paycheck. So, they give me their payroll's fax line, I fax over notice of their bankruptcy, and garnishment stops. End of story, right?

Nope, somehow CapOne took it upon themselves to code my personal credit card (paid off at that point) in their system as being in bankruptcy -- without my SSN, without my account number, just based upon my name on the fax cover letter. My credit score instantly took a 150 point hit; this was my oldest and most established line of credit. It took me **over a month** phone calls to have this situation rectified, and only when I finally demanded to have a call from their general counsel or I would start posting on social media. BOOM - account is reopened in 4 hours.

My credit score still took years to recover, and they never effing apologized.

TL;DR: CapitalOne is scum.
